title: The Image of God: A Bible Study on Human Worth
subtitle: A five-session study on the imago Dei and the dignity it gives every person.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has ever wondered what a human being is worth, and why, and who is tired of hearing the answer either inflated into flattery or shrunk down to chemistry. It walks slowly through five sessions on the oldest and most radical claim the Bible makes about people, that they are made in the image of God. It begins where the doctrine begins, in Genesis 1 and a single sentence that was closer to sedition than to compliment in the world that first heard it, because every empire around Israel kept the divine image locked in the palace and Genesis took it out and handed it to everyone. It moves through the three classic accounts of what the image is, and why the argument is not a seminary parlor game but a matter of who gets counted as fully human. It faces the fall honestly, the image defaced and never erased, and then follows the whole doctrine to the place it was always pointing, to Christ, who is not a bearer of the image but the image itself, and into whose likeness the broken image is being remade. It ends in the street, where the doctrine has to live or die, with the poor and the unborn and the enemy and the stranger and the person who annoys you, every one of them stamped with a worth you did not assign and cannot revoke.

This is not a study that admires human dignity from a safe height. The writer came to faith from atheism, which means he spent years holding the other answer, that a human being is a clever animal and nothing more, and he knows from the inside how thin that answer turns out to be when you are standing at a hospital bed or a graveside. He was raised without a father and is raising five sons, and he writes as a man who has both doubted his own worth and quietly assigned worth to others on a sliding scale, generous to the useful and stingy toward the inconvenient. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you, because the doctrine of the image is the one teaching in Scripture that will not let you look down on a single human being without looking up into the face of the God who made them, and it turns out that the people we find easiest to despise are the ones this doctrine was written to protect.
audience: Adults, small groups, and anyone wrestling with human worth and dignity

sessions.title: The Image the Kings Kept for Themselves
sessions.aim: To read Genesis 1:26-27 in the world that first heard it, to see what the word image claimed against every empire around Israel, and to grasp that the doctrine took the divine image out of the palace and handed it to everyone, refusing both the flattery that makes the image a compliment to human greatness and the reduction that makes the human one more animal.
sessions.summary: Bell says the first thing to understand about the sentence is how dangerous it was to say out loud. Then God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. We hear a warm compliment, a pat on the human head, and we miss that in the world it was first spoken into it was closer to sedition. Every civilization surrounding Israel had a doctrine of the divine image, and every one of them kept it in the palace. In Egypt the Pharaoh was the image of the god, the living statue of the deity walking among men. In Mesopotamia the king was the image of the god, his representative on the earth, and no one else was. The image was a title of empire, a way of saying that one man carried the divine on his face and the rest of the race existed to serve him. That is the world Genesis 1 walks into, and it does something with the doctrine that should still stop us. It takes the image out of the palace and gives it to everyone, to the slave and the woman and the infant and the enemy, male and female, all of them the image and likeness of God. J. Richard Middleton calls this the liberating image, and the word is exact. Bell takes the strong case for the modern reduction, that a human is a highly evolved animal and the talk of a divine image is a flattering story we tell ourselves. He grants what is true in it. But the reduction cannot explain why we keep behaving as though people matter infinitely when our own account says they do not. The image is not a compliment we pay ourselves and not a capacity we can lose. It is a status conferred by God, a vocation to represent him, given to every human before any of them had done a thing to earn it.

keyScripture.why: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them, naming every human being, and not merely the king or the strong or the useful, as the bearer of the divine image, and including the woman in the same breath the ancient world never did.

discussion.q: Bell says that in the ancient world only the king was the image of the god, and Genesis takes that title and hands it to everyone. What changes about the sentence when you hear it as a challenge to empire rather than a compliment to humanity?
discussion.behind: Open by relocating the text into its own world before anyone applies it. Most people have only ever heard the image as a nice thing said about human beings in general. Help the room feel the scandal, that the doctrine was a demotion of every king and a promotion of every nobody, and that this was political and dangerous before it was ever devotional. Land it on the reversal, not yet on the application.

discussion.q: The Hebrew word for image, tselem, is used elsewhere for a statue set up to represent a god in a temple. If every human is God's statue placed in the temple of his creation, what is a person for?
discussion.behind: Press on the vocation buried in the word. A statue in the ancient temple was where you went to see what the god looked like and to meet the god's presence. Help the room hear that being the image is not first a fact about human insides but a job, to make the invisible God visible, to represent him in the world he made. Do not resolve the three views yet, just surface that the image points beyond the self.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for the reduction, that a human being is a clever animal and the divine image is a flattering story. What is honestly true in that account, and where does it fail to explain how we actually live?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness and honor the skeptic in the room. The evolutionary continuity with the animals is real, and Scripture never denies that humans are creatures formed from dust. Grant it fully. But the reduction cannot account for why we treat human worth as non-negotiable, why we are outraged by cruelty in a way we are not by a lion killing a gazelle. Let the gap sit open rather than rushing to close it.

discussion.q: Genesis includes male and female in the image in the same sentence, which the surrounding cultures never did. Why does it matter that the image was democratized to include exactly the people the ancient world counted as lesser?
discussion.behind: Draw out the reach of the democratization. The image is given not to the powerful but across every line the ancient world used to rank people, and it lands first on those the world discounted. Help the room see that this is the seed of every later claim about human equality, and begin, gently, to ask who they still quietly rank, because the doctrine names them too.

discussion.q: Bell says the image is not a compliment we pay ourselves or a capacity we can boast, but a status God conferred before we had done anything to earn it. Where have you treated your own worth as an achievement, and how would it change you to receive it as a gift?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. Most of us live as though our worth is earned, tied to what we produce or how we perform, which is exhausting and also secretly proud. Invite each person to notice the ledger they keep on themselves, and let the conferred, unearned image land as relief. Go first if the room is slow, and name your own performance treadmill.

objections.objection: The image of God is just a prescientific way of flattering ourselves. We now know human beings are one more species of animal, produced by the same evolutionary process as everything else, and dressing that up as a divine image is wishful thinking.
objections.response: Grant the continuity honestly, because Scripture grants it too. Genesis says the human is formed from the dust of the ground, a creature among creatures, and the biology that links us to the animals is real and not a threat to the doctrine. Concede all of it. Where the reduction fails is not in what it affirms but in what it cannot explain, which is why the person making the objection still lives as though people possess a worth that atoms and instincts cannot deliver. He is outraged by injustice, grieved by cruelty, convinced that a child matters more than a stone, and none of that follows from the premise that a human is only a clever animal. The image is the missing explanation, not a flattering story but the only account that makes sense of the dignity everyone already assumes and no one can build from below. You do not have to believe it to notice that your own moral life is written in its language.

objections.objection: If the image is really about a vocation to represent God and rule the creation, then it sounds like a license for humans to dominate and exploit the planet, which is exactly what has gone wrong.
objections.response: Take the ecological grief seriously, because it is pointing at a real and grievous abuse of the text. The dominion of Genesis 1 has been read as a warrant to plunder, and the reading has done damage, and no honest study should pretend otherwise. But look at what the word actually means in its own world, because the king who was the image was not licensed to strip the land, he was held responsible to represent the god's own care for it, to rule as the god would rule. To bear the image is to be answerable to the One imaged, which is the opposite of a blank check. The human is placed in the garden to work it and keep it, the same verb used for guarding something precious. Dominion in the image is not ownership, it is stewardship exercised on behalf of a King who called the creation good and will ask what we did with it. The abuse is real, and it is a violation of the vocation, not the vocation itself.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose face is hardest for you to see the image of God in, and what does that difficulty tell you about the worth you have quietly been assigning to people?
sessions.practice: This week, pick one person you tend to look past or look down on, the clerk, the panhandler, the relative who wears on you, and before you interact, say to yourself the plain fact that this person is the image of God, God's own statue in the world. Do not announce it. Just let the sentence sit under the encounter and notice what it does to how you speak and look. Write down what changed in you when you treated an ordinary person as the bearer of the divine image rather than as a fixture in your day.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made a world of kings who kept the divine image locked in their palaces, and then you did the unthinkable and stamped it on everyone, the slave and the woman and the infant and the stranger, all of them your image and likeness. Forgive us for shrinking that gift back down, for treating our own worth as a thing we earned and other people's worth as a thing we grade. Teach us to see your face where we have trained ourselves not to look. Make us the statues you set us up to be, showing the world what you are like. We did not give ourselves this dignity and we cannot revoke it in anyone else. Let that truth reorder how we treat every person we meet this week. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated the image of God in myself as an achievement to defend rather than a gift I was given?
Who are the people I have quietly ranked as less than fully human, and what standard have I been secretly using to do it?
If a human being is God's statue set up to show the world what he is like, what has my life been showing the world about him?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the first thing to understand about the sentence is how dangerous it was to say out loud. Then God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. We hear a warm compliment, a religious pat on the human head, and by hearing it that way we miss almost everything, because in the world it was first spoken into the sentence was closer to sedition than to flattery. Every great civilization that surrounded ancient Israel had a doctrine of the divine image, and this is the part we forget, every single one of them kept it in the palace. In Egypt the Pharaoh was the image of the god, the living statue of the deity walking the earth, his rule an extension of the god's rule and his person a kind of visible divinity. In Mesopotamia the king was the image of the god, planted on the earth as the god's representative, and the ordinary human being was not. The image was a title of empire. It was a way of saying that one man, at the top, carried the divine on his face, and that the rest of the human race, the farmers and the slaves and the women and the conquered, existed to serve the one who did. That is the world Genesis 1 walks into, and we have to feel the weight of that world to feel what Genesis does inside it. Because Genesis takes the doctrine of the divine image, the most exclusive and aristocratic idea in the ancient Near East, and it detonates it. It takes the image out of the palace and it hands it to everyone. Not to the king. To the human being as such. To the slave who owns nothing and the woman the culture counted as property and the infant who has done nothing and the enemy on the far side of the river, male and female, all of them, without exception and without hierarchy, made in the image and likeness of God. The scholar J. Richard Middleton, in his study of Genesis, calls this the liberating image, and the word is precise, because what Genesis performs is a liberation, a stripping of the divine dignity from the one and a bestowing of it on the all. Look closely at the word itself, because it carries the point. The Hebrew is tselem, and it is the ordinary word for a statue, the kind of carved image a people would set up in a temple to represent their god, the place you went to see what the god was like and to meet his presence among you. Genesis is saying that the human being is that, God's statue, set up not in a building made of stone but in the whole temple of his creation, placed here to represent him, to make the invisible God visible, to show the watching world what the true King is like. Which means from the very first page the image is not mainly a fact about what is inside you. It is a vocation. It is a job. It is the dignity of being the one creature commissioned to stand in for God in the world he made. Now take the strong case against all of this, because a thoughtful skeptic makes it and I made it myself for years before I believed anything. The modern reduction says that all this talk of a divine image is a flattering story a clever animal tells itself, that human beings are one more species produced by the same blind process as every other, formed from the same dust, running on the same instincts, and that the image of God is a comforting fiction we drape over our fear of being nothing. Grant what is true, because a great deal is, and Scripture grants it first. The human really is a creature, formed from the ground, kin to the animals, mortal and made of dirt, and the Bible never once pretends otherwise. But watch where the reduction breaks, because it breaks on the person making it. The one who says a human is only a clever animal does not live as though that were true for one waking hour. He is outraged by cruelty, grieved at a graveside, certain that a child is worth more than a stone and that some things must never be done to a person no matter how useful it would be. None of that follows from his premise. You cannot get infinite human worth out of atoms and appetite. The image is the missing explanation, the only account that makes sense of the dignity every one of us already assumes and none of us can build from the ground up. And here is where I have to stand inside it rather than above it. The doctrine does not only rescue the beggar from my contempt. It exposes me, because I have spent my life quietly assigning worth on a sliding scale, generous toward the useful and the impressive and the people who can do something for me, and stingy, dismissive, barely seeing, toward the inconvenient and the ordinary and the ones who cost me something. I have treated my own dignity as an achievement I earned and other people's as a grade I was entitled to assign. The image will not allow either. It was conferred, not earned, given to every human before a single one of them had done a thing to deserve it, which means I cannot inflate my own and I cannot dock anyone else's. The kings kept the image for themselves. God gave it away. And the first thing that gift does, before it comforts you, is take out of your hand the ruler you have been using to measure other people.

scriptureStudy.note: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion. The image and the dominion arrive together, so representing God and ruling on his behalf are one vocation. The human is made to stand in for the King, not to be one.

In the image of God he created him, male and female he created them. The verse says it twice for emphasis and then does the radical thing, folding male and female into the same image in the same breath, dignifying exactly the half of humanity the ancient world discounted.

Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it. The blessing spreads the image across the whole race and down every generation. The dominion is given to all of them together, never to one ruler over the rest, which is the liberation Genesis performs.

The Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. The same creature who bears the image is made of dirt. Scripture holds both without embarrassment, dust and glory in one body, so the image is never a denial of our creatureliness.

The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. The verb for keep is the word for guarding something precious. Dominion in the image is stewardship on behalf of the King, answerable to him, the opposite of a license to exploit.

What is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. The psalm marvels at exactly the paradox, a dust creature crowned with royal dignity by God's own choice.

You have given him dominion over the works of your hands, you have put all things under his feet. The royal vocation of Genesis is sung back to God, confirming that the image is a conferred kingship exercised under the true King, held in trust and not in possession.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the ancient background the session only sketches, because the more you learn about the world Genesis wrote into, the more startling the text becomes. In both Egyptian and Mesopotamian royal ideology, the language of the divine image was reserved almost entirely for the king, and it did real political work, legitimizing his absolute rule as the earthly presence of the god. J. Richard Middleton, in The Liberating Image, argues in detail that Genesis 1 is a deliberate counter-statement to this ideology, a polemic that takes the royal-functional image and universalizes it to all humanity, and a group willing to sit with his case will see the creation account as far more subversive than the tame reading allows. Set this beside the observation, which many scholars make, that the making of humans is narrated differently from everything else in Genesis 1, with the divine deliberation, Let us make man, marking the human as the summit and purpose of the whole ordered creation. A group should weigh, carefully and without overreaching, how much of the modern conviction of universal human equality is historically downstream of this text, since the ancient world it entered simply did not hold that all humans were of equal worth, and the idea had to come from somewhere. Then take the harder theological turn, holding the functional reading against the classical one rather than pretending the debate is settled, which is the work of session two. Notice that even here in session one the image is presented less as a thing humans possess than as a status God assigns and a task God gives, which quietly guards the doctrine against the trap it most often falls into, grounding human worth in a capacity that some humans have more of than others. The aim is not to master the scholarship for its own sake but to let the strangeness of the text in its own world break the flatness of the reading we inherited, so that the sentence recovers the danger it had when it was first written down.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is successful, capable, and quietly runs his whole life on merit. When the session lands on the image as a conferred and unearned dignity, he does not resist the theology, but you can see it does not reach him, because he has always assumed, without ever saying it, that worth is something you produce, that a person is valuable in proportion to what they contribute. He is generous, he works hard, and he has no idea that his generosity is a form of condescension, help extended downward from a man secretly certain he is worth more. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it presses him. His diligence is real and good, and the world needs people who carry weight. But notice the ruler he is using, because the merit standard that inflates his own worth is the same standard that silently discounts everyone who produces less, the disabled, the elderly, the struggling, the poor. The danger of his position is not that he values excellence. It is that he has grounded human dignity in a capacity, and any dignity grounded in a capacity can be lost, and will be denied to whoever falls below the line he has drawn. Do not let him reduce the doctrine to a nice sentiment he can affirm without cost. Honor his labor fully, and still ask him, gently, whether he could receive his own worth as a gift he did not earn, because until he can, he will keep grading everyone he meets.

sessions.title: What the Image Is, and Why the Argument Matters
sessions.aim: To learn the three classic answers to what the image actually is, the substantive, the functional, and the relational, to see the strength and the danger in each, and to grasp that this is not a seminary parlor game but the argument that decides who gets counted as fully human.
sessions.summary: Bell says that for two thousand years the church has agreed that human beings bear the image of God and disagreed about what the image is, and that the disagreement is not a footnote, because the answer you give decides who you are willing to treat as fully human. There are three classic answers, and each has held the loyalty of great minds. The substantive view says the image is a quality inside us, most often reason or the rational soul, and it runs from Augustine and Aquinas down through most of Christian history. The functional view says the image is a role, the vocation to represent God and rule the creation as his stewards, and it fits the ancient royal background best. The relational view says the image is found in relationship, in our being made for God and for one another, and it belongs to Karl Barth and Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who located the image not in a capacity we possess but in the relationships in which we stand. Bell takes the strong case for the substantive view, because it is the historic majority and it honors something real, that humans reason and choose in a way animals do not. He grants its dignity. But he names its danger plainly, and it is a lethal one. If the image is a capacity like reason, then whoever has less of the capacity has less of the image, and history is a catalog of the horrors that follow when someone decides another group does not measure up. The functional and relational views guard against this, because a vocation can be given to a person who cannot exercise it and a relationship can hold a person who cannot respond. The truest answer holds all three together, but it holds them in an order, and the order is the whole point. The image is first something God gives and does, not something we possess and perform, which means it cannot be graded, and no one falls below the line.

keyScripture.why: When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God, and then Adam fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, tying the image to what is simply passed from parent to child, given and inherited rather than achieved, which cuts against any view that grounds it in a capacity a person might lack.

discussion.q: Before tonight, if someone had asked you what the image of God actually is, what would you have said? Which of the three views, a quality inside us, a role we are given, or a relationship we stand in, were you unknowingly assuming?
discussion.behind: Surface the working answer before naming the options. Most people have an unexamined instinct, usually the substantive one, that the image means human reason or soul or free will. Get it into the open without correcting it yet. The point is to show that everyone already holds a view, and that the view has been quietly shaping who they count as fully imaging God.

discussion.q: Bell says the substantive view, that the image is reason or the rational soul, has a lethal danger hidden in it. If the image is a capacity, what happens to the person who has less of that capacity, and where have you seen that logic play out?
discussion.behind: Press on the stakes, carefully, because this is tender ground where real families and real grief live. Help the room see the trap, that grounding worth in a capacity means worth can be lost or denied, and that this is not abstract. It is the logic behind every dehumanization, the disabled, the demented, the unborn, the enemy declared less than human. Hold it pastorally, but do not soften the danger.

discussion.q: The functional view says the image is a vocation to represent God, and the relational view says it is found in our relationships with God and each other. How does each of these protect the worth of someone who cannot reason, in a way the substantive view struggles to?
discussion.behind: Draw out the pastoral payoff of the other two views. A vocation can be assigned to a person who cannot yet or can no longer carry it out, and a relationship can hold a person who cannot respond, the way a parent's love holds a newborn or a spouse holds someone lost to dementia. Help the room feel why the argument is not academic, it is the difference between dignity that can be revoked and dignity that cannot.

discussion.q: Bell says the truest answer holds all three views together but in an order, with what God gives and does coming before what we possess and perform. Why does the order matter so much, and what goes wrong when we put our performance first?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center. If the image is first a gift and a call from God's side, it cannot be graded by our capacities, and every human holds it fully. If we put the capacity first, we are back to ranking. Help the room see that the order is not a compromise but a safeguard, and that it mirrors the whole gospel, grace before response, gift before work.

discussion.q: If you are honest, whose full humanity do you find it easiest to doubt, the person with severe disability, the one deep in dementia, the criminal, the unborn, the enemy? What view of the image have you been quietly running to justify the doubt?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication. Everyone draws a line somewhere, a category of person whose full worth they privately question, and everyone has a theory that lets them do it. Invite honest confession without shaming, and let the room see that the substantive instinct, worth by capacity, is usually the tool. Go first, and name your own line, because the leader is inside this too.

objections.objection: This is exactly the kind of hair-splitting that makes people tune out. Does it really matter whether the image is a quality or a role or a relationship, as long as we agree people have dignity? It sounds like theologians inventing a debate to stay employed.
objections.response: Feel the impatience, because it is honest and it is aimed at a real vice, the theology that argues over definitions while people starve. Grant that the church has wasted itself on distinctions that changed nothing. But this is not one of them, and here is how you know. The moment a society has to decide whether the person in the persistent coma, or the fetus, or the prisoner, or the enemy is fully human and fully protected, it reaches, whether it knows it or not, for a theory of what makes a human count. If the answer is a capacity, reason or self-awareness or usefulness, then the line can always be moved, and history shows it always is, and the people on the wrong side of it are always the weak. The argument about what the image is turns out to be the argument about who lives with dignity and who can be discarded. It is the least abstract question in the room. The definition is where the protection is either grounded or lost.

objections.objection: If the image is really just a role or a relationship and not something actually in us, then it seems like empty words. Either humans genuinely are different from animals in their nature, or the whole thing is a label with nothing behind it.
objections.response: Honor the instinct, because it is protecting something true. There is a real difference between humans and animals, and the substantive view is right to insist on it, and no honest account should flatten it. Concede that. But notice the false choice hiding in the objection, that the image is either a possession inside us or an empty label, as if a gift and a relationship were nothing. A newborn is fully a son or a daughter before it can do anything a child does, and the relationship is not empty, it is the most real thing about the child, and it holds when every capacity fails. The relational and functional views do not empty the image, they anchor it somewhere sturdier than a faculty that can be damaged or lost. And the deepest reason to prefer that anchor is not tidiness, it is love, because a dignity grounded only in a capacity abandons exactly the people, the infant and the disabled and the dying, whom this doctrine was written to protect.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you been grounding your own worth, and the worth of the people you love, in a capacity that can be lost, and what would it mean to ground it instead in what God gives and cannot take back?
sessions.practice: This week, find the place where your own theory of the image is doing quiet damage, the relative you have written off, the group you have decided are less, the version of yourself you value only when you are producing. Name which view you have been running, worth by capacity, worth by usefulness. Then deliberately treat one such person, or yourself, as fully imaging God regardless of what they can do. Write down what it exposed in you to ground someone's worth in God's gift rather than in their performance.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you made us in your image and then let us spend two thousand years arguing about what that means, and somewhere in the arguing we found ways to decide that some people image you more than others. Forgive us. Forgive the theories we have built to justify looking down on the weak, the slow, the unborn, the enemy, the ones whose capacities do not measure up to ours. Teach us that the image is your gift before it is our possession, your call before it is our performance, so that it cannot be graded and no one falls below the line. Anchor our worth, and the worth of every person we are tempted to discount, in what you give and will not take back. And where we have drawn a line through the middle of the human race, give us the grace to erase it. Amen.
reflection: Which of the three views of the image have I been unknowingly living by, and who does that view allow me to discount?
Have I grounded human worth, my own and others, in a capacity that can be lost, or in what God gives and cannot revoke?
Where is the line I have drawn between the fully human and the less-than, and what would it cost me to let the doctrine erase it?
sessions.teaching: Bell says that for two thousand years the church has agreed on one thing and argued about another. It has agreed that human beings bear the image of God. It has argued, without ceasing, about what the image actually is. And it would be easy to file that argument under the harmless disputes of theologians, the sort of thing that fills seminary seminars and changes nothing, except that it is not harmless at all, because the answer you give to what the image is turns out to decide who you are willing to treat as fully human. Get this wrong and people die for it. So we have to walk, slowly and fairly, through the three classic answers, because each of them has held the loyalty of serious and faithful minds, and each of them sees something the others can miss. The first is the substantive view, and it is the historic majority report. It says the image is a quality, a property, a something located inside the human being, and most often that something is named as reason, the rational soul, the capacity to think and choose and know God. Augustine found the image in the mind, in memory and understanding and will. Thomas Aquinas located it in the intellect, the rational nature that sets the human apart from the beasts. For most of Christian history this is what educated believers meant by the image, the God-given faculty of reason and moral will that no animal shares. And there is real truth in it, real dignity, because human beings do reason and create and deliberate in a way nothing else in the visible world does, and any account that denies this is lying about what a person plainly is. Grant the substantive view its due. But now name its danger, and do it plainly, because it is a lethal one and it has killed. If the image is a capacity like reason, then the image comes in degrees, because capacities come in degrees. And if the image comes in degrees, then some people have more of it and some have less, and the person whose reason is impaired, the infant who cannot yet think, the man lost to dementia who no longer knows his own name, the profoundly disabled child who will never form a sentence, has, on this logic, less of the image, and therefore, the logic whispers, less of the worth. This is not a hypothetical horror. It is the actual machinery of every dehumanization in human history. Decide that the image is a capacity, and you have handed the powerful a ruler with which to measure the weak and find them wanting, and they always do. This is why the second and third views matter so much, because they were recovered, in part, to shut that door. The functional view, which fits the ancient royal background we saw last session, says the image is not mainly a quality inside us but a vocation given to us, the calling to represent God and to rule his creation as his stewards. And notice what this does. A vocation can be given to someone who cannot presently carry it out. A king's infant son is fully the heir before he can lift the scepter, and a title held in trust is held completely even by the one who cannot yet exercise it. The third view, the relational, belongs above all to Karl Barth and to Dietrich Bonhoeffer, and it locates the image not in what we possess but in the relationships in which we stand, our being made for God and made for one another. Barth read the male and female of Genesis 1 as the clue, the image found in the I and the Thou, in the human made not to be alone but to be in relationship, corresponding to the relationship God himself is. Bonhoeffer, lecturing on Genesis in the years the Nazis were building their catalog of the less-than-human, refused to let the image be a possession at all and called it instead a relation, a being-free-for God and for the other, established by God from his side. And see what the relational view protects. A relationship can hold a person who cannot respond. The newborn is fully loved before it loves back. The husband keeps the covenant with the wife who no longer knows him. If the image is the relationship God establishes toward us, then it holds when every human capacity has failed, because it never depended on the capacity in the first place. Take the strong case for the substantive view one more time, because I do not want to dismiss the majority of the church as simply wrong. Humans really do reason, and the fact matters, and a purely functional or relational account can drift into vagueness if it denies that there is anything distinctive in human nature at all. So the truest answer does not pick one and discard the others. It holds all three. But, and this is the whole point, it holds them in an order. What God gives and does comes first, before what we possess and perform. The image is first a status God confers and a call God issues and a relationship God establishes, and only after that, downstream and secondary, the capacities by which we live it out. Put the order that way and the doctrine is safe, because a gift cannot be graded and a call does not depend on the strength to answer it and a relationship holds the one who cannot respond. Put the order the other way, capacity first, and you are back to ranking human beings by their faculties, which is where the killing starts. And I have to say that I have run the wrong order in my own heart more than I want to admit, quietly valuing people by what they can do, sharpest toward the ones who could think with me and slowest to see the full humanity of the ones who could not. The argument about what the image is looked like a parlor game. It turns out to be the argument about whether the weakest person in the room is as fully human as I am. Genesis has already answered. Adam fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and the image went to the child before the child had done a thing, passed down like a family face, given and never earned.

scriptureStudy.note: When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Written after the fall, the verse still calls fallen humanity the likeness of God, which means the image survived, and it is stated as a plain given about the species, not a prize for the capable.

Adam fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The image is passed from parent to child like an inherited face, received before the child can do anything, which cuts against any view that grounds it in an achieved or exercised capacity.

For God made man in his own image. Spoken to Noah after the flood, over sinful humanity, it grounds the sanctity of every human life in the image that fallen people still bear, protecting the person by their status and not by their merit or ability.

You formed my inward parts, you knitted me together in my mother's womb, I am fearfully and wonderfully made. The psalmist's worth is grounded in God's making and knowing of him, before and beneath any capacity he could exercise, a dignity assigned in the womb.

With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. James assumes ordinary, present, fallen human beings still bear the likeness, which is why cursing them is an offense, the image held by all and not measured out by degree.

The new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. Paul ties the image to knowledge of God, honoring what the substantive view saw, while making it a thing being renewed by grace rather than a possession we generate, which keeps the order right.

God chose what is foolish, weak, and low in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are. God's habit of exalting the discounted is the death of every scheme that ranks human worth by capacity, and the vindication of the weak the substantive view endangers.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the history of the three views with more care, because knowing where each came from helps a group hold them without caricature. The substantive reading dominated the tradition from the Fathers through the medievals and into the Reformers, with Augustine locating the image in a trinitarian structure of the soul, memory, understanding, and will, and Aquinas grounding it in the rational intellect, and it is worth granting that this reading was trying to honor a real datum, the God-directedness of human reason, rather than merely to flatter the clever. The functional view is the one most modern Old Testament scholarship, including Middleton, judges closest to the meaning of Genesis 1 in its own world, and a group should weigh how much of the older substantive reading was shaped by later Greek philosophical categories imported into the text rather than drawn from it. The relational view is the great twentieth-century recovery, and here the reading and the moment cannot be separated, since Karl Barth developed it in Church Dogmatics as Europe was organizing itself around a doctrine of racial hierarchy, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer lectured on the image in Creation and Fall in 1932 and 1933, in Berlin, as the regime that would murder him was constructing its own catalog of lives unworthy of life. A group willing to sit with that will understand that the relational and functional recoveries were not academic fashions but, in part, theological resistance, the church relocating human dignity somewhere the state could not reach it, out of the capacities a regime could measure and into the gift and call of God. Then press the constructive question this platform lands on, which is not which view wins but in what order they are held. Test the claim that the tradition went wrong most often not by choosing a view but by putting human capacity first in the order, and that the safeguard against every dehumanization is to insist that the image is first what God gives, does, and calls, and only secondarily what we possess and perform. The aim is a group that can hold the genuine insight of all three, refuse the false choice between them, and see clearly why the order, grace before capacity, is not a theological nicety but the wall that stands between the weak and those who would rank them out of the human race.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group has a brother with a profound intellectual disability, a man in his forties who cannot speak, cannot care for himself, and will never do what the world calls productive work. She has sat through years of Christian talk about the image of God as human reason and rationality, and every time she has felt something go cold in her, because she has heard it, correctly, as a doctrine that leaves her brother out. When the session names the danger of the substantive view, she does not feel attacked, she feels, for the first time, defended. Here is the work for the leader, and it is mostly to let the doctrine do its healing. Do not rush past her to be balanced. Honor first what she has seen more clearly than the theologians, that a worth grounded in capacity is a worth her brother can never have, and that this is not a small flaw in the view but a wound it has inflicted on families like hers. Then let her hear the functional and relational answer as the good news it is, that her brother is fully the image of God, given a status he did not earn, held in a relationship with God he did not initiate and cannot lose, as much God's own statue in the world as any professor. Her brother does not have less of the image because he can do less. He bears it whole. Let her carry that home, and let the room learn from her that the argument about the image was never abstract to the people it was written to protect.

memoryVerse.text: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.

sessions.title: Defaced but Not Destroyed
sessions.aim: To face the fall honestly, to see what sin did to the image and what it could not do, and to hold together two truths the church keeps pulling apart, that the image is real and grievously marred, and that it was never erased, so that human dignity survives even our worst.
sessions.summary: Bell says the doctrine of the image has two enemies, and they sit on opposite sides of the room. One side is so impressed with human dignity that it cannot take sin seriously, and the other is so impressed with human sin that it forgets the dignity, and the fall is the place where both go wrong. The real question is what sin actually did to the image, and Scripture gives a careful, two-sided answer that neither side likes. The image was defaced. Genesis 3 is not a minor stumble but a catastrophe, the creature made to represent God deciding to be God, and the ruin is real and total in its reach, touching the reason and the will and the relationships the image was made to hold. Bell takes the strong case for the darkest reading, the one that says the image is so corrupted as to be as good as gone, and he grants the seriousness the reading is defending, because the church has often been far too cheerful about human nature. But he shows where it breaks, on the plain testimony of Scripture itself, because after the fall, after the flood, over murderers and sinners, God still calls the human being his image. Genesis 9 grounds the sanctity of life in the image of fallen people. James says the tongue curses those made in God's likeness, meaning ordinary, sinful people now. The image is defaced, and the image is not destroyed, and the whole pastoral weight of the doctrine hangs on holding both. Then the turn. The dignity that survives is not a scrap of goodness we can boast in. It is a wound and a signature at once, a ruined greatness that explains why human evil is so uniquely terrible and why no human being, however far gone, is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

keyScripture.why: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image, spoken to a world washed clean of almost everyone for its violence, grounding the protection of every remaining sinful life in an image the fall marred but never erased.

discussion.q: Bell says the doctrine of the image has two enemies, one that takes dignity so seriously it forgets sin, and one that takes sin so seriously it forgets dignity. Which of those two errors is more natural to you, and how does it show up?
discussion.behind: Open by helping each person locate their own tilt. Some people are congenital optimists about human nature and flinch at the word sin, others are so convinced of human depravity that they can barely see any glory left. Both are half-truths. Get the room to name which half they overplay, because the fall is exactly where the two errors have to be corrected by each other.

discussion.q: Genesis 9 grounds the command against murder in the fact that God made man in his own image, and it says this to survivors of a flood sent because of human violence. Why does God protect the sinner by pointing to the image, and what does that tell you about how far the image survives?
discussion.behind: Press on the astonishing placement of the verse. God has just judged the earth for its wickedness, and the first thing he does is protect human life by appealing to the image, in people who have proven capable of terrible evil. Help the room see that the image is not a reward for the righteous but a status that clings to the sinner, which is why even the worst human life is under God's protection.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for the darkest reading, that sin has corrupted the image almost to nothing. What is that reading rightly protecting, and what does Scripture say that it cannot fully account for?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves with care. The dark reading is defending the seriousness of sin against a sentimental culture that will not name evil, and it is right that the corruption is total in its reach. But it cannot account for Genesis 9 and James 3, which speak of the image as a present possession of fallen people. Help the room grant the seriousness while refusing the conclusion that the image is gone.

discussion.q: Bell calls the dignity that survives the fall a wound and a signature at once, a ruined greatness. How does seeing human beings as defaced royalty change the way you understand both human evil and human worth?
discussion.behind: Draw out the both-and at the heart of the session. Human evil is uniquely terrible precisely because it is committed by image-bearers, greatness gone wrong, not an animal following instinct. And human worth survives precisely because the image, though marred, remains. Help the room feel that the ruin and the dignity are not in tension but explain each other, and that this is a truer account of people than either optimism or cynicism.

discussion.q: Is there a person, or a version of yourself, you have quietly written off as beyond worth, beyond change, past the point where the image could still be there? What has believing that let you do, or stop doing?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, gently, because this can touch real despair. We write people off, and we write ourselves off, and the writing-off is always a denial that the image survives. Handle with care for anyone carrying shame about themselves or grief over someone lost to addiction or hardness. Let the truth that the image is not destroyed land as hope, and keep a path to help visible. Go first with your own too-far-gone verdict.

objections.objection: How can you say people still bear the image of God after everything human beings do to each other? Look at history, the genocides, the cruelty, the abuse. If that is the image of God, the image is either a lie or an insult to God.
objections.response: Do not argue with the horror, sit inside it, because the objection is not being cynical, it is being honest about evil in a way the sentimental never are. The catalog of human cruelty is real and it is worse than the objector says, and any doctrine that makes light of it is false. Concede the darkness completely. But notice what the objection assumes and cannot explain, that this cruelty is a horror at all. We are not outraged when a spider eats its mate, because we expect nothing else of a spider. We are undone by human cruelty precisely because we know, underneath our theories, that a human being was made for more, that this is greatness in ruins and not an animal being an animal. The image is exactly what makes human evil so uniquely terrible. A defaced masterpiece grieves us in a way a blank wall never could. The evil does not disprove the image. It is the desecration of it, and the grief you feel is the image in you recognizing the ruin of the image in them.

objections.objection: This sounds like a way of letting people off the hook. If everyone still has this precious image no matter what they do, then where is accountability? It seems to excuse the worst behavior by insisting on some hidden dignity underneath it.
objections.response: Hear the concern for justice, because it is right that a cheap dignity which excuses evil would be a moral disaster, and Scripture never offers one. The image does not lessen guilt, it deepens it. To sin as an image-bearer is worse, not better, than to sin as a mere animal, because it is a betrayal of what you were made to be and to show, and the murder condemned in Genesis 9 is condemned precisely because the victim bore the image. So the doctrine is not soft on evil, it is the ground of taking evil seriously at all. What the surviving image refuses is not accountability but despair, the conclusion that a person is finished, beyond worth and beyond hope, fit only to be discarded. You can hold a person fully accountable for what they have done and still refuse to say they are no longer human. Justice names the wrong. The image insists the wrongdoer is still a someone God made, still under his protection, still not past the reach of his mercy. Both, or you have lost the gospel.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where has your sense of your own failure convinced you that the image in you is destroyed rather than defaced, and what would change if you believed God still sees his own likeness in you?
sessions.practice: This week, hold together the two truths this session refuses to separate. Toward one person you have been too soft on, yourself included, name the sin honestly rather than excusing it, because the image makes evil serious. Toward one person you have written off as beyond change or beyond worth, refuse the verdict, and treat them as defaced royalty rather than as ruined and finished. Write down which was harder for you, naming the sin or refusing to write someone off, because the harder one shows which of the two errors is yours.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we come as your defaced image, and we do not know which is harder to believe, that we are so ruined or that we are still yours. We have taken the greatness you gave us and turned it against you and against each other, and the wreckage is real, and we will not pretend it is small. But you would not let go of your likeness in us. You protected the sinner and the murderer by pointing to the image they still bore, and you have never once looked at a human being, however far gone, and called them past worth or past hope. Give us your two-eyed sight, to name evil as the desecration it is and to refuse to write off a single person you have not written off. Where we have despaired of ourselves or of someone we love, remind us that a defaced image is not a destroyed one, and that you are in the business of restoring what we ruined. Amen.
reflection: Do I take sin seriously enough to grieve it, or do I explain human evil away because I am too impressed with human dignity?
Do I take the image seriously enough to refuse writing anyone off, or am I so impressed with human sin that I forget the dignity that survives?
Where have I believed the image in me is destroyed rather than defaced, and what has that despair cost me and the people around me?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the doctrine of the image has two enemies, and the trouble is that they sit on opposite sides of the same room and each thinks the other is the only danger. On one side is the person so impressed with human dignity that he cannot take sin seriously, who hears the word depravity as an insult to the human spirit and believes, at bottom, that people are basically good and just need the right conditions. On the other side is the person so impressed with human sin that he has forgotten the dignity entirely, who has read the news and read his own heart and concluded that the talk of a divine image is a pious fiction laid over a fundamentally rotten thing. And the fall, Genesis 3 and everything that pours out of it, is the exact place where both of them go wrong, because Scripture's account of what sin did to the image is careful and two-sided and refuses to comfort either one. So we have to ask the real question plainly. What did sin actually do to the image of God in us? And the answer has two parts, and you cannot drop either without lying. The first part is that the image was defaced, and defaced is not too strong. Genesis 3 is not a small misstep, not a regrettable lapse in an otherwise upward climb. It is a catastrophe. The creature made to represent God reached instead to replace him, to be God rather than to image God, and the ruin that followed is real and it is total in its reach. Not total in the sense that nothing good remains, but total in the sense that nothing was left untouched. The reason that was meant to know God now rationalizes and deceives. The will that was meant to love God now curves in on itself. The relationships the image was made to hold, with God, with each other, with the creation, all of them fractured in the same afternoon, the man and the woman hiding, blaming, exiled, and their firstborn a murderer before the second chapter of the human story is done. Anyone who tells you the fall was minor has not read the account and has not read himself. Take the strong case for the darkest reading of all, because faithful people have held it and it is defending something the church desperately needs to keep. That reading says the corruption is so deep that the image is as good as gone, effectively destroyed, that fallen man is so far from God that whatever is left of the likeness is a ruin not worth the name. And I want to grant what this reading is protecting, because it is protecting the seriousness of sin against a culture, and a church, that will do almost anything to avoid the word. We are sentimental about human nature in a way that would have baffled every previous Christian century, and the dark reading is a needed cold water in the face. But here is where it breaks, and it breaks not on my preference but on the plain words of Scripture. Because after the fall, after the whole race has proven what it is, after a flood sent because the earth was filled with violence, God speaks to the survivors and grounds the sanctity of human life in the image, present tense, in these sinners, these murderers, these people who have just demonstrated exactly how far the corruption goes. Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. If the image were destroyed, that sentence is nonsense. It is not nonsense. It is the charter of human dignity, and God speaks it over fallen people. And centuries later James, writing to Christians about the sins of the tongue, says we bless God and curse people who are made in the likeness of God, and he means ordinary, present, sinful human beings, right now, still the likeness. So hold the two truths, because the whole pastoral weight of the doctrine hangs on holding both at once. The image is defaced. The image is not destroyed. Marred, but not erased. And now the turn, because the dignity that survives is not a happy scrap of leftover goodness we can point to and feel better about ourselves. It is something stranger and more useful than that. It is a wound and a signature at the same time, a ruined greatness, defaced royalty. And once you see human beings that way, two things you could never explain before come clear. First, you understand at last why human evil is so uniquely and specifically terrible, why we are undone by cruelty in a way we simply are not by a predator killing its prey. It is because human evil is greatness gone wrong, the image desecrated, a masterpiece slashed, and the grief we feel is the right response to a defacement, not to an animal being an animal. Second, you understand why no human being is ever beyond worth or beyond hope. If the image were destroyed, then some people really could be written off, past saving, fit only to be discarded, and every one of us keeps a private list of exactly such people, and I have kept mine. But a defaced image is still an image. The signature is still under the ruin. Which means the worst person you know, and the worst version of yourself you have buried in shame, is not finished, not past worth, not beyond the reach of the God who has never yet looked at his defaced likeness and decided it was not worth restoring. And that is precisely where the doctrine is going, because a defaced image raises a question it cannot answer on its own. It can survive. It cannot repair itself. For that we need not a better version of ourselves but the true image, the one who came to make the ruined ones new.

scriptureStudy.note: You will be like God, knowing good and evil. The fall is the image-bearer reaching to be God rather than to represent him, the vocation inverted at the root. The defacing begins not with a small sin but with the creature grasping the Creator's place.

The man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God among the trees of the garden. The first fruit of the fall is a broken relationship, the very thing the relational view says the image is for, so sin strikes the image exactly where it lives.

Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him. Within a generation the image-bearer is a murderer, spilling the blood of another image-bearer, which shows the ruin is real and total in reach, touching even the first family God made.

For God made man in his own image. Spoken after the flood over sinful survivors, it proves the image was not destroyed by the fall, since the protection of human life still rests on an image that fallen people demonstrably still bear.

Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. David names the depth of the corruption without ever concluding he is not God's, holding sin's seriousness and his own worth before God together, which is the balance the session defends.

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. The glory we fall short of is the glory we were made to bear and reflect, so the verse assumes both the original dignity and its present ruin, defaced greatness stated in a single line.

With it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. My brothers, these things ought not to be so. James assumes fallen people presently bear the likeness, and makes the surviving image the reason our contempt for them is sin. The image protects the sinner from us.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the theological history the session compresses, because the church worked hard to hold the two-sided truth and the vocabulary it developed is worth learning. The Reformed tradition, following Calvin, spoke of the image in a broad sense and a narrow sense, the broad image being the constitution of humanity that survives the fall, reason, conscience, relationship, the vocation to rule, and the narrow image being the original righteousness, knowledge, and holiness that were lost in the fall and are restored only in Christ. A group that grasps this distinction will see how Scripture can say both that the image remains, Genesis 9 and James 3, and that it must be renewed, Colossians 3 and Ephesians 4, without contradiction, because it is speaking of the image in these two senses. Calvin himself wrote that the image was not utterly annihilated and destroyed but so corrupted that what remains is a frightful deformity, and that phrase holds the balance the session is after, a real image, really defaced. Set this against the older debate the Fathers had over image and likeness, some reading them as two distinct things, the image retained and the likeness lost, a reading most modern interpreters set aside as reading too much into a Hebrew poetic parallelism, and a group can weigh why the church sometimes built large structures on small grammatical foundations. Then take the pastoral and historical turn that matters most, testing the claim that both errors, the sentimental and the cynical, are not merely intellectual mistakes but have real-world consequences. A theology that forgets the fall produces a church that cannot name evil, that offers the anxious and the guilty cheap comfort and calls it grace, the therapeutic religion that has become the actual folk faith of much of the culture. A theology that forgets the surviving image produces a church that can write people off, that despairs of the addict and the prisoner and the enemy, that loses the ground for pursuing the lost. The aim is a group that can hold Calvin's frightful deformity in one hand and God's protected image in the other, taking sin with a seriousness the culture has abandoned and refusing the despair that abandons people, because only that two-eyed sight prepares the way for the restoration the next session brings.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group carries a specific and heavy shame. Years ago he did something he considers unforgivable, a betrayal that cost him a marriage and the trust of his children, and though he has been a believer since, he has quietly concluded that whatever he was made to be, he has destroyed it, that the image in him is not defaced but demolished. When the session insists the image is marred and never erased, you can see him resisting it, because his despair has become a strange kind of comfort, a way of not having to hope. Here is the work for the leader, and it must be gentle and unhurried, and it must not rush him past his real grief. Do not minimize what he did, because the doctrine does not, and a cheap word here would insult both his conscience and his victims. The image makes his sin serious, and pretending otherwise would not help him. But press, kindly, on the lie hidden in his despair, that he has the power to destroy what God made and God protects, which is a strange inversion of pride, as if his sin were stronger than God's likeness. It is not. The image in him is ruined, not gone, and a ruined image is exactly the kind of thing the true image came to restore. Keep a path to real help visible, a counselor, a pastor who can walk with him. Honor the weight he carries, and still refuse, on God's behalf, to agree that he is finished, because God has not agreed to it.

memoryVerse.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.

sessions.title: The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming
sessions.aim: To see that the whole doctrine of the image was always pointing forward to Christ, who is not a bearer of the image but the image itself, and to grasp that salvation is the defaced image being remade into his likeness, so that Christian formation is nothing less than becoming truly human at last.
sessions.summary: Bell says that everything so far has been building to a name, and that the doctrine of the image cannot be finished in Genesis because it was never meant to end there. Adam was made in the image. Christ is the image. The difference is the whole gospel. Paul does not say Jesus bears the image well or reflects it clearly. He says he is the image of the invisible God, the one in whom the God no eye has seen is finally made visible, the true and original of which Adam was only ever the copy. The real question is what this does to us, and the answer runs in two directions at once. Backward, it tells us that Adam was always pointing to Christ, that the human race was made in the image of the Son before the Son ever took our flesh. Forward, it tells us where salvation is actually going, because Paul says believers are being conformed to the image of the Son, remade after the image of their creator, changed into his likeness from one degree of glory to another. Bell takes the strong case for the objection that this makes Christianity a program of self-improvement, becoming a better version of yourself, and he grants why it looks that way. But he shows the difference, and it is total. This is not the self polishing the self. It is the defaced image being restored by the true image, from the outside in, by grace and by beholding, not by effort and by striving. Then the turn that reframes the whole Christian life. To be saved is not to become something other than human. It is to become human at last, to have the ruined likeness remade into the likeness of the one who wore our flesh without ruin. The image was defaced in a garden. It is restored in a Person.

keyScripture.why: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, naming Christ not as one more image-bearer but as the image itself, the true original in whom the unseen God is made visible, and the pattern into which the defaced human image is being remade.

discussion.q: Paul says Christ is the image of the invisible God, not merely someone who bears it well. What changes when you hear that Jesus is the true original and Adam, and you, were the copy?
discussion.behind: Open on the distinction that reorganizes everything. We tend to think of Jesus as the best example of an image-bearer, a human who got it right. Paul says something far stronger, that Christ is the image itself, the original. Help the room feel that this makes Christ not our best member but our source and pattern, the one Adam was always a copy of, which reframes both who Jesus is and who we are.

discussion.q: Bell says salvation is not becoming something other than human but becoming human at last. How does it change your sense of the Christian life to hear that being conformed to Christ is the same thing as being made truly human?
discussion.behind: Draw out the reframe at the heart of the session. Many people carry a quiet sense that holiness means becoming less themselves, more restrained, more religious. Paul says it is becoming what humanity was always meant to be. Help the room hear formation not as subtraction but as restoration, the ruined image remade, so that the most Christlike person is also the most fully human.

discussion.q: Paul says we are changed into his image from one degree of glory to another by beholding the glory of the Lord. Why beholding, and not mainly striving? What does it mean that we become like what we look at?
discussion.behind: Press on the mechanism, because it cuts against the works instinct. Paul grounds the change not in effort but in beholding, in fixing our gaze on Christ, because we are made to become like what we worship and attend to. Help the room examine what they actually behold all day, the screens, the ambitions, the fears, and consider that they are being formed into the image of whatever holds their gaze.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that this all sounds like self-improvement, becoming a better version of yourself. Where is that reading tempting, and what makes restoration by the true image completely different from polishing the self?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves honestly. The language of change and growth can sound exactly like the self-help culture, and a group should feel the pull of that reading. But the difference is total, because the source is outside us, Christ restoring his own defaced image by grace, not the self improving the self by effort. Help the room see that one ends in exhaustion or pride and the other in gratitude and rest.

discussion.q: If Christian formation is the true image being restored in you, where do you see the restoration actually happening, and where are you still trying to do it yourself by striving rather than by beholding?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication and honesty. Everyone has areas where grace is visibly remaking them and areas where they are white-knuckling their own improvement and calling it sanctification. Invite honest naming of both, without shame for the striving, and point the room back toward beholding Christ rather than watching themselves. Go first, and name where you are still striving.

objections.objection: Being conformed to the image of Christ just sounds like religious self-improvement with extra steps. Every self-help book tells you to become your best self, and this is the same thing dressed in Bible language, the endless project of fixing yourself.
objections.response: Grant why it looks identical from the outside, because the vocabulary really does overlap, both talk about change and growth and becoming, and the church has often preached sanctification in a way indistinguishable from a self-help seminar with prayer attached, so the suspicion is earned. But the two are opposites at the root, and the root is where they differ. Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same broken thing straining to fix itself by effort, which ends either in the exhaustion of failure or the pride of apparent success, and both are prisons. What Paul describes runs the other way entirely. The self does not restore the image, the true image restores it, from outside, by grace, and the means is not striving but beholding, being changed into his likeness by looking at him rather than by working on ourselves. One is a mirror in which you watch yourself and try harder. The other is a window through which you behold Christ and are quietly remade by what you see. The difference is not the amount of effort. It is the direction the power comes from.

objections.objection: If Jesus is the true image and we are being conformed to him, does that not erase everyone's individuality? It sounds like the goal is for all Christians to become identical copies of the same person, which is exactly the conformity that makes religion frightening.
objections.response: Hear the fear of a crushing uniformity, because it is a real fear and some religion has earned it, producing people who are eerily the same, their edges sanded off into a single approved shape. Concede that this is a genuine danger and a real distortion. But look at what conformity to Christ actually produces, because it is the opposite of what the objection fears. When the image is restored, people do not become less themselves, they become more, because sin is the great flattener, the thing that makes us all predictable in our selfishness, all running the same tired scripts of pride and fear. Holiness is where genuine variety appears, because a person set free from having to protect and promote themselves is finally free to be the particular, unrepeatable person God made them. The saints are not identical. They are the most vividly themselves of anyone who has ever lived. Christ is not a cookie-cutter pressed down on every face, he is the source in which each face at last becomes fully its own. Conformity to him is the death of the sameness, not its triumph.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What are you actually beholding most hours of your day, and if it is true that you become like what you look at, what are you being slowly formed into?
sessions.practice: This week, change one thing you behold. Find a stretch of time you normally give to a screen or a worry, and instead spend it looking at Christ, in a Gospel, reading slowly, watching how he treats people, letting your gaze rest on him rather than on yourself. Do not turn it into a project you grade. Just behold, and let the beholding do its work. Write down whether it is harder for you to stop striving and simply look, and what that difficulty reveals about where you have been trying to restore yourself by effort.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you are the image of the invisible God, the true original that Adam was only ever a copy of, and you wore our flesh without ruining it and now you are remaking the ruin in us. Forgive us for turning your work of grace into a project of self-improvement, for standing at the mirror straining to fix ourselves when you called us to the window to behold you and be changed. We become like what we look at, and we have been looking at everything but you. Turn our gaze. Restore your defaced image in us not by our striving but by your grace, from one degree of glory to another, until we are at last what you made us to be, truly human, fully alive, unmistakably ourselves and unmistakably yours. We cannot repair what we ruined. You can. You are. Amen.
reflection: Have I been treating the Christian life as self-improvement, the self working on the self, or as the true image restoring his likeness in me by grace?
What do I actually behold all day, and what is it forming me into, since I become like what I look at?
Where am I striving to fix myself at the mirror when Christ is calling me to the window to behold him and be changed?
sessions.teaching: Bell says everything in this study so far has been building to a name, and that the doctrine of the image cannot possibly be finished in Genesis, because it was never meant to end there. Genesis gives you the image made and Genesis 3 gives you the image defaced, and if that were the whole story it would be a tragedy with no third act, a masterpiece slashed and left slashed. But the New Testament picks up the word image and does something with it that changes the entire doctrine, and it does it by attaching the word to a name. Adam was made in the image of God. Christ, Paul says, is the image of God. And that one-word difference, made in versus is, is the whole gospel. Listen to how Paul actually says it, because we soften it out of habit. He does not say that Jesus bears the image well, or reflects it more clearly than the rest of us, or is the best example of what an image-bearer should look like. He says he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. He says elsewhere that Christ is the light of the gospel of the glory of God, who is the image of God. The writer of Hebrews says he is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature. This is not the language of a good copy. This is the language of the original. The God no eye has ever seen, the invisible One, is made visible in Jesus, not partially, not approximately, but exactly, so that when Philip says show us the Father, Jesus can answer that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. And here is what that does, running in two directions at once. Run it backward first. If Christ is the true image, then Adam was always the copy, and the astonishing implication that Paul draws out is that the human race was made in the image of the Son before the Son ever took on our flesh. We were patterned after him. He is not a late addition to the story of humanity, a rescue operation improvised after the fall. He is the template we were struck from in the beginning, which means the most human face that ever existed is his, and every other human face, including Adam's before he fell and yours now, is a likeness of that face. Now run it forward, because this is where the doctrine reaches into your actual life. Paul tells us exactly where salvation is going, and he tells us in the language of the image. Those God foreknew, he says, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. You have put on the new self, he says, which is being renewed after the image of its creator. And the most beautiful sentence of all, that we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being changed into his image from one degree of glory to another. So the defaced image is not left defaced. It is being restored, and it is being restored into the likeness of the true image, the Son. Take the strong case against all of this, because it is the obvious modern objection and it deserves a real answer. It sounds like self-improvement. It sounds like Christianity is one more program for becoming the best version of yourself, the same project every self-help book on the shelf is selling, just with Bible verses stapled to it, the endless exhausting labor of fixing yourself. And I grant why it looks that way, because the church has often preached it exactly that way, sanctification as a self-improvement seminar with prayer attached, and the suspicion is fair. But the two things are opposites at the root, and the root is the only place that matters.
