Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same broken and defaced thing straining to repair itself by its own effort, and that project has only two possible endings, the exhaustion of failing at it or the pride of seeming to succeed, and both of them are prisons. What Paul describes runs the other direction entirely. The self does not restore the image. The true image restores it, from the outside, by grace. And notice the means Paul names, because it is not striving, it is beholding. We are changed into his likeness by beholding the glory of the Lord, which is to say, by looking at him. We become like what we look at. We are formed into the image of whatever holds our gaze, and this is the most practical thing in the whole doctrine, because it means the question of your formation is largely the question of your attention. What are you beholding, hour after hour, day after day? Because you are being slowly and surely conformed to it. The self-improver stands at a mirror, watching himself, straining, grading, trying harder, and stays the same tired self. The Christian stands at a window, beholding Christ, and is quietly remade by what he sees. One is effort aimed inward. The other is attention aimed at him. And now the turn that reframes the entire Christian life, the thing I most want to leave you with. We think of being saved as becoming religious, or becoming better, or becoming something other than what we are. It is none of those. To be conformed to the image of Christ is to become human at last. The most Christlike person you have ever met was also the most fully alive, the most genuinely themselves, the least flattened and least false. Because sin is what made us less than human, the defacing of the thing we were made to be, and its restoration is not the addition of a religious layer on top of a human life. It is the healing of the humanity itself. The image was defaced in a garden, by a creature grasping to be God. It is restored in a Person, the true God who became the true man, and who is even now, by grace and by the long slow work of our beholding him, remaking his ruined likeness in everyone who looks.

scriptureStudy.note: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. Christ is not a bearer of the image but the image itself, the true original in whom the unseen God is made visible, the pattern after which humanity was made and into which it is remade.

The light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. The gospel is precisely the shining out of the image, and Satan's work is to blind people to it, which tells you the image of God in Christ is the very thing salvation makes us see.

He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature. The word for imprint is the stamp left by a seal, an exact impression, so Christ is not a rough likeness of God but the precise and full expression of who God is.

Predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. The goal of salvation is stated as conformity to the image of the Son, so being remade into Christ's likeness is not a side effect but the very point of being saved.

Beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. The change comes by beholding, not by striving, and it is gradual, from glory to glory, the defaced image restored by grace through a fixed and worshipful gaze.

The new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator. Salvation is described as the renewal of the image, present and ongoing, so the Christian life is the restoration project of the ruined likeness, done by grace and never finished in a day.

Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. The restoration is not only present but final, ending in the full bearing of Christ's image at the resurrection, the ruined likeness not merely repaired but glorified.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the biblical theology that ties the image to Christ across the whole canon, because seeing the thread changes how you read Scripture. The pattern is often called the Adam-Christ structure, drawn most explicitly by Paul in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, where Adam is the first man and Christ the last Adam, the head of a new humanity, so that the image defaced in the first is restored in the second. A group willing to trace this will see that the doctrine of the image is not a static fact about human nature but a moving story with a beginning, a rupture, and a restoration, and that Christ stands at the center as both the origin and the goal. Set this against the older observation that the New Testament never speaks of Christ being made in the image, as Genesis says of Adam, but of Christ being the image, and weigh the theological weight of that grammatical difference, that Adam is a likeness while Christ is the reality, the true of which Adam was the type. Then take up the mechanism of change the session names, becoming like what we behold, which is not a modern psychological insight bolted onto the text but a thoroughly biblical one, running from the Psalms, where those who make idols become like them, to Paul's beholding in 2 Corinthians, to John's promise that when Christ appears we shall be like him because we shall see him as he is. A group should sit with the sobering flip side, that the same law by which we are conformed to Christ by beholding him is the law by which we are deformed into the image of whatever else we worship, so that the attention economy that fractures our gaze is not spiritually neutral but formative, shaping us into the image of what holds our eyes. The aim is to let the doctrine reframe the whole Christian life as restoration rather than self-improvement, to ground that restoration entirely in Christ the true image and in grace received rather than effort exerted, and to press the intensely practical question of what, in fact, each person is beholding, since that is what they are becoming.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group is one of the most disciplined believers you know, and she is exhausted. She reads her Bible on a strict schedule, tracks her spiritual habits, measures her growth, and treats her sanctification like a fitness plan, always monitoring whether she is improving. She has heard sermons on being conformed to Christ and received them as marching orders, one more standard to meet, and the striving has left her weary and quietly joyless, because no matter how hard she works, the self she is watching in the mirror never quite becomes what she is aiming at. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor her devotion before it redirects it. Her hunger for God is real and her discipline is not the problem, and you must not shame the diligence, because a lazy alternative would help no one. But notice where her gaze is fixed, because she is standing at the mirror, watching herself, grading her own progress, and the whole weight of her formation is resting on her own effort. That is self-improvement wearing the clothes of sanctification, and it will exhaust her because it was never meant to carry the weight she has put on it. Do not tell her to try less. Tell her to look elsewhere, to move from the mirror to the window, from watching herself improve to beholding Christ, and to trust that the change comes from him by grace, from one degree of glory to another, while she looks at him rather than at herself. Honor her love for God fully, and still lift the crushing project off her back, because the true image is the one doing the restoring, and she was never the one holding it together.

memoryVerse.text: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.

sessions.title: The Image in the Street
sessions.aim: To bring the whole doctrine down into daily life, where it has to live or die, and to see that if every human being bears the image of God, then the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, and the person who annoys you carry a worth we did not assign and cannot revoke, so that how we treat them is how we treat their Maker.
sessions.summary: Bell says the doctrine of the image is either the most practical thing in the Bible or it is nothing, because a truth about human worth that stays in the head and never reaches the street was never believed in the first place. The real question is not whether we affirm the image but whether we can see it in the specific faces we would rather not, and James puts the knife exactly there. With the same tongue, he says, we bless God and curse people made in his likeness, and we do not even notice the contradiction, because the person we are cursing does not look like the image to us. So the session walks down the list of the people the image most inconveniently covers. The poor, whom Proverbs says we insult our Maker by despising. The unborn, whom the psalmist says God knits together and knows before a capacity is exercised, and whom this doctrine dignifies with a care the study handles honestly and without turning a person in crisis into a slogan. The enemy, whom Christ commands us to love precisely because our Father makes his sun rise on them too. The stranger, whom the law commands Israel to love as themselves. And the person who simply annoys us, which may be the hardest of all, because contempt does its quiet work below the level of anything we would call hatred. Bell takes the strong case for the objection that this is politically convenient for one side, and he refuses it, insisting the image cuts against every tribe, the one that discards the unborn and the one that discards the immigrant and the prisoner and the enemy, with the same blade. Then the ending, which does not resolve. If the image is real, there are no ordinary people, no disposable ones, no faces safe to despise. You have never locked eyes with a mere mortal. Every person you passed today was the image of God, and you will answer for how you saw them.

keyScripture.why: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God, exposing the contradiction at the center of ordinary religious life, that we honor God with our words and dishonor his image in the very next breath, and never notice the two are the same act.

discussion.q: James says we bless God and curse people made in his likeness with the same tongue and do not notice the contradiction. Whose face does not look like the image of God to you, and what lets you curse them without feeling you have done anything wrong?
discussion.behind: Open by putting the knife where James puts it. The point is not that we openly deny the image but that we contradict it without noticing, because certain people simply do not register to us as image-bearers. Get the room to name, honestly, the specific category of person they discount, and to see that cursing them and blessing God are, James says, the same tongue doing opposite things.

discussion.q: Bell walks down the list, the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, the person who annoys you. Which one of those is hardest for you to see the image in, and why that one?
discussion.behind: Get specific, because the doctrine only bites at the level of the particular. Everyone finds one category hardest, and it is usually the one their tribe has trained them to discount. Help each person name their own hardest case without immediately defending themselves, and notice that the hardest face is exactly the one the image was written to protect from them.

discussion.q: Proverbs says whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, and Christ says what you did to the least of these you did to him. What does it do to your treatment of the poor and the overlooked to hear that you are treating their Maker that way?
discussion.behind: Press on the vertical dimension of horizontal treatment. Scripture keeps saying that how you treat the image is how you treat the One imaged, so contempt for a person is contempt aimed, whether you mean it or not, at God. Help the room feel the weight of that, that there is no such thing as a private unkindness to an image-bearer, without letting it collapse into guilt that changes nothing.

discussion.q: Bell insists the image cuts against every tribe, the one that discards the unborn and the one that discards the immigrant, the enemy, and the prisoner, with the same blade. Where is it convenient for your side to forget the image, and can you name it as honestly as you name the other side's blind spot?
discussion.behind: This is the hardest and most necessary question, and it must fire in both directions. The temptation is to wield the image against the other tribe and exempt your own. Hold the room to the discipline of naming their own side's discarded people, not just their opponents'. Self-implicate first as the leader, and refuse to let the doctrine become a weapon for one political team.

discussion.q: Bell ends by saying you have never locked eyes with a mere mortal, that every person you passed today bore the image of God. Who did you look past or look down on this week, and how would that encounter have gone differently if you had seen them as the image of God?
discussion.behind: Close on the concrete and the convicting, and let it land without resolving. Bring it all the way down to actual faces from an actual week, the clerk, the driver, the relative, the stranger. Let the room feel the weight of how many image-bearers they moved through without seeing, and send them out carrying it rather than relieved of it. End in weight, as the doctrine does.

objections.objection: Using the image of God to talk about the unborn or the immigrant is just baptizing a political agenda. This is religion picking a side in the culture war and pretending God signed off on its voting guide.
objections.response: Take the suspicion seriously, because it is often deserved, since the image of God has been conscripted into partisan projects on every side, quoted to win an argument rather than to see a person, and that misuse is real. But test the charge against what the doctrine actually does, because a political agenda is selective and the image is not. The agenda of the right forgets the image in the immigrant, the prisoner, the enemy, the refugee, and the agenda of the left forgets it in the unborn, and the doctrine of the image indicts both with exactly the same blade, which is precisely what no political tribe will do. If a teaching only ever convicts the other side, it has become a tribe wearing the robes of orthodoxy, and you are right to distrust it. But a doctrine that makes you defend the very people your own team discards is not a political weapon, it is the death of political weapons, because it refuses to let any tribe reduce a human being to their usefulness for its cause. The image does not pick your side. It stands over every side and asks whether you can see the face your politics taught you to look past.

objections.objection: It is naive and even dangerous to talk about seeing the image of God in your enemy. Some people are genuinely evil and want to do harm, and telling victims to see the divine image in their abuser is exactly how the church has kept people trapped in danger.
objections.response: Concede the danger immediately and completely, because this warning is protecting real and vulnerable people, and any teaching that uses the image to send a victim back into harm is a wicked distortion of it. To see the image in someone does not mean trusting them, staying in reach of them, or declining to protect yourself or others from them, and where there is abuse the loving and faithful thing is safety, distance, and help, not a sentimental blindness dressed as love. Grant all of that without hedging. But hear the distinction the doctrine draws, because it is exactly the one that keeps love from curdling into either denial or hatred. Seeing the image in an enemy does not mean pretending they are not dangerous, it means refusing to let even a genuine enemy become, in your eyes, less than human, a thing rather than a person, because the moment they do, you have begun to lose your own humanity to your hatred. You can name someone's evil clearly, protect yourself from it fully, work for justice against it, and still refuse to forget that the one who does it is a defaced image-bearer and not a mere monster. That refusal is not for their sake alone. It is what keeps the fight against evil from turning you into it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose face have you allowed your politics, your fear, or your grievance to erase, so that they no longer register to you as the image of God, and what would it cost you to see them again?
sessions.practice: This week, take the one category from the list you found hardest, the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, or the person who simply annoys you, and do one concrete thing that treats that person as the image of God rather than as a problem, a threat, or a fixture. Not a grand gesture. One real act of seeing. And if the hardest one is closest to home, the relative or coworker who wears on you, start there. Write down what it exposed in you to honor the image in the exact person you had trained yourself not to see.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we bless you with our mouths and curse your image with the same breath, and the terrible thing is that we do not even notice. We have looked past the poor and looked down on the stranger and hardened ourselves against the enemy and let the people who annoy us stop being people at all. And we have let our tribes tell us which image-bearers count, defending the ones it is convenient to defend and discarding the rest with a clear conscience. Forgive us. Give us back our sight. Let us see your face in the clerk and the immigrant and the prisoner and the child not yet born and the enemy across every line we have drawn. Teach us that there are no ordinary people, no faces safe to despise, no one we can treat with contempt without treating you so. We have never once locked eyes with a mere mortal. Do not let us forget it again. And where there is real danger, give wisdom that protects even as it refuses to hate. Amen.
reflection: Whose full humanity have I let my tribe, my fear, or my grievance erase, and can I name my own side's discarded people as honestly as I name my opponents'?
Do I believe that how I treat the image is how I treat the One imaged, and would this week look different if I did?
How many image-bearers did I move through this week without seeing, and what would change if there really are no ordinary people?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the doctrine of the image is either the most practical thing in the whole Bible or it is nothing at all, because a truth about human worth that lives comfortably in the head and never once walks down into the street was never actually believed. You can affirm the image of God in a small group and go home and treat the drive-through worker like a vending machine and the relative you cannot stand like weather and the enemy on the far side of your politics like a category rather than a face, and if you do, you did not believe the doctrine, you only agreed with it, which is a different and cheaper thing. So this last session is the test, and the test is not whether you can define the image but whether you can see it, in the specific people you would rather not. James puts the knife exactly there, and he twists it. With the same tongue, he says, we bless our Lord and Father, and with the same tongue we curse people who are made in the likeness of God, and here is the part that should keep us up at night, we do not even notice the contradiction. We do not feel the whiplash of praising God in one breath and despising his image in the next, because the person we are cursing simply does not look like the image to us. That is the whole problem in one sentence. The image is real, and our eyes have been trained not to see it on certain faces. So let us walk down the list of exactly those faces, the people the doctrine most inconveniently covers. Start with the poor, because Scripture is relentless here. Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, says the Proverb, and whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker, and Jesus takes it further than we are comfortable with, saying that what we did, or failed to do, for the least of these, the hungry and the imprisoned and the stranger, we did or failed to do for him. There is no private contempt for a poor man. It travels straight up to the God whose image he is. Then the unborn, and I want to handle this one with care rather than as a slogan, because behind the abstraction are real women in real crisis and the doctrine is not served by cruelty. But the psalmist says plainly that God formed his inward parts and knitted him together in his mother's womb and knew him there, before he had reasoned a thought or performed a use, which means the worth of the unborn rests exactly where the worth of the disabled and the dying rested in our earlier sessions, not on a capacity achieved but on a God who assigns dignity in the dark before anyone can earn it. If worth waits on usefulness, the smallest and least useful lose it first. Then the enemy, and this is where the doctrine stops being agreeable, because Christ commands us to love our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, and he grounds the command in the image, in the Father who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good alike. To see the image in an enemy is not to pretend they are safe, and where there is real danger the faithful thing is protection and not sentiment, but it is to refuse to let even a genuine enemy become, in your eyes, less than human, because the moment they do, your hatred has begun to deface the image in you. Then the stranger, the foreigner, the one not from here, whom the law of Israel commands them to love as themselves, remembering that they too were once strangers in a land that was not theirs. And then the last one, and it may be the hardest of all, the person who simply annoys you. Not the dramatic enemy, not the tragic poor, just the coworker whose voice grates and the relative whose opinions exhaust you and the man talking too loudly three tables over. Because contempt does its quiet work far below the level of anything we would ever call hatred, in the eye-roll and the sigh and the thousand tiny dismissals by which we file a fellow image-bearer under nuisance and stop seeing them as a person at all. Now take the strong case against all of this, the objection I most need to answer honestly, that this is politically convenient, that using the image to talk about the unborn or the immigrant is just religion baptizing one side's agenda. And I refuse it, flatly, and here is how you know the refusal is honest. The image cuts against every tribe with the same blade. It indicts the side that discards the immigrant and the prisoner and the enemy, and it indicts the side that discards the unborn, and it will not let either one exempt itself. That is precisely what no political agenda will ever do, because an agenda is selective and the image is not. If a doctrine only ever convicts the people you already disagree with, it has stopped being orthodoxy and become a tribe in robes, and you should distrust it. The image is the death of the tribal weapon, because it forces you to defend the very people your own side has agreed to throw away. And I have to say this stands over me too, because I find some of these faces genuinely easy and others genuinely hard, and the hard ones are not random, they are the ones my own instincts and my own tribe have trained me to look past, and the doctrine keeps dragging my eyes back to exactly them. So here is where it ends, and it does not end tidily, because this doctrine does not resolve, it convicts and then sends you out still carrying it. If the image is real, then there are no ordinary people. There are no disposable ones. There is no face anywhere that is safe to despise. C. S. Lewis said it as well as it has ever been said, that you have never talked to a mere mortal, that next to the Blessed Sacrament itself your neighbor is the holiest object presented to your senses. Every person you passed today, the one who annoyed you and the one you pitied and the one you feared and the one you did not see at all, was the image of God, defaced and dignified, made and loved and known. You will answer, one day, for how you saw them. So the only honest question to carry out of five weeks on the image is not whether you believe it. It is whose face you are going to go home and finally see.

scriptureStudy.note: With it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. James makes cursing a fellow human an offense against the image they bear, and exposes the unnoticed contradiction of blessing God and despising his likeness with the same tongue.

Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him. How we treat the poor travels directly up to God, because the poor bear his image, so contempt for them is an insult aimed, whether we intend it or not, at their Maker.

Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. The sanctity of every human life, and the seriousness of taking it, rest on the image, which is why the doctrine is the ground of all human rights and not a sentiment.

You knitted me together in my mother's womb, your eyes saw my unformed substance. God's knowing and forming of the person in the womb, before any capacity, grounds the worth of the smallest and least useful exactly where every image-bearer's worth rests, in God's assigning.

Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father, for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good. Christ grounds enemy-love in the Father's own regard for the image even in those who hate him.

You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself. The law extends the full dignity of the neighbor to the foreigner, refusing to let belonging or origin determine whose image is honored.

As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. Jesus identifies himself with the hungry, the sick, the imprisoned, and the stranger, so that treatment of the least visible image-bearer is treatment of the King himself.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session gestures at, because the claim that all human beings possess equal dignity is far stranger and more fragile than we assume, and knowing its roots helps a group defend it. The historian and the philosopher alike have traced how the conviction of universal human equality, now treated as self-evident, is in fact historically downstream of the biblical doctrine of the image, since the ancient world that surrounded the church simply did not hold that a slave and an emperor, a barbarian and a citizen, an infant and an adult were of equal worth, and the idea had to be introduced against the grain of the culture. A group can weigh the sobering argument, made even by some secular thinkers, that a thoroughly secular account struggles to ground the very human dignity it wants to keep, that the branch of universal worth may be sitting on a root of the image it has cut away. Set this against the twentieth century's testimony, Dietrich Bonhoeffer resisting a regime built on a doctrine of lives unworthy of life, and Martin Luther King drawing the case for civil rights straight from the image of God stamped on every person, and notice that in each case the doctrine did political work precisely by refusing to belong to any political tribe, indicting the powerful in the name of a dignity they did not confer and could not revoke. Then take the hardest pastoral turn, testing the discipline this platform insists on, that the doctrine must cut against one's own side as sharply as against the other. A group should practice this honestly, naming the specific image-bearers their own political and cultural tribe finds it convenient to discard, not only the ones their opponents discard, because the moment the image becomes a weapon aimed in a single direction it has been captured by a tribe and emptied of its power. The aim is not to arrive at a voting guide but to recover the doctrine as the ground of a dignity that stands over every human being and under no party's control, and to send each person back into an ordinary week newly unable to look past the faces they had trained themselves not to see, because a doctrine of the image that changes no encounter on Monday was never believed on Sunday.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group is warm, generous, and deeply committed to justice for the causes her community cares about, and she speaks movingly about the dignity of the poor and the immigrant and the prisoner. But when the session names that the image cuts against every tribe, including her own, and mentions the unborn in the same breath as the immigrant, you can feel the room tighten, because for her these belong to different and opposed moral worlds, and to name them together feels like a betrayal of her side. Here is the work for the leader, and it requires the same even-handedness the doctrine demands, and it must honor her real compassion before it presses her. Her care for the discarded is not a pose, it is a genuine fruit of seeing the image, and you should say so warmly, because a study that only convicted her side would be committing the exact tribalism the session condemns. But the whole point of the image is that it does not respect the borders our tribes draw, and the discipline she rightly applies to her opponents' blind spots is the discipline the doctrine now asks her to apply to her own. Do not let her hear this as an ambush from the other team, because it is not, and the leader must be just as willing to press the opposite blind spot in the man across the circle whose compassion runs strong for the unborn and thin for the prisoner and the enemy. Honor her love for the overlooked fully, and still ask her, gently, whether she can name her own side's discarded image-bearers as clearly as she names the other side's, because the image belongs to no party, and the moment it becomes a weapon for hers, she has lost it.

memoryVerse.text: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.

leaderPrimer: The particular danger of a study on the image of God is that it is the easiest doctrine in the world to affirm and the hardest to actually believe, and a room can spend five weeks agreeing warmly that all people bear the image while quietly exempting the specific people each person finds it convenient to discount. If you let it, this study becomes a group congratulating itself on a high view of human dignity in the abstract while never once being made to see the face it looks past every Monday. So set the aim the first night and hold it every night after. This is not a study about human worth in general. It is a study about whether you can see the image of God in the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, and the relative who exhausts you, and the only person whose sight anyone is responsible for in this room is their own. Guard against two failures especially. The first is the tribal capture of the doctrine, and it is the most likely one, because the image of God has been conscripted by every political side to defend the people it already wanted to defend and to indict only its opponents. Refuse this from the front, and refuse it in both directions, and refuse it in your own heart first, because a leader who wields the image against the other team and exempts his own will teach the room to do the same, and the doctrine will be lost in the very session that names it. The second failure is turning a doctrine of worth into a weight of guilt that changes nothing, five weeks of feeling bad about how we treat people and no actual person seen differently. Keep driving the sessions down to the concrete, to real faces from a real week, because the image is either the most practical doctrine in Scripture or it is nothing. Take special care in two places. Session three touches real despair, people who have written themselves off as beyond worth or beyond change, and session five touches the unborn and the enemy, where there are almost certainly people in the room carrying private grief, a crisis pregnancy in the family, a wound from an abuser, a loss. Handle both with care, keep a path to real help visible, know a counselor and a pastor you can point to, and never let the doctrine be used to send anyone back into harm, because seeing the image in a dangerous person never means staying in reach of them. Bell leads this from inside it. He came to faith from atheism, so he knows the other answer from the inside, and he confesses that he still assigns worth on a sliding scale, generous to the useful and stingy toward the inconvenient. If you present yourself as the one who already sees every face rightly, the room will perform agreement back at you and no one's eyes will open. Go in as a person still learning to see, still catching yourself looking past the image. Five weeks will not make anyone love perfectly. It can send a room home unable to look at a single human being the same way again, which, for this doctrine, is the only success there is.

faq.q: Is this study going to get political, especially on things like abortion and immigration?
faq.a: It refuses to be captured by any political side, and that refusal is the whole discipline. The doctrine of the image cuts against every tribe with the same blade, indicting the side that discards the immigrant and the prisoner and the enemy, and the side that discards the unborn, and it will not let either one exempt itself. Session five names this directly and holds the leader to firing the conviction in both directions, including at their own side first. The aim is never a voting guide. It is to recover a human dignity that stands over every political party and belongs to none of them, so that a person leaves less able to look past the specific faces their own tribe taught them to discount. If a teaching on the image only ever convicts the people you already disagree with, it has stopped being orthodoxy and become a tribe in robes, and this study is built to refuse exactly that.

faq.q: What does the image of God actually mean? I have heard it my whole life and could not really explain it.
faq.a: You are in good company, because the church has agreed for two thousand years that humans bear the image and argued the whole time about what it is. Session two walks through the three classic answers. The substantive view says the image is a quality inside us, usually reason or the soul. The functional view says it is a vocation, the calling to represent God and steward his creation. The relational view says it is found in our relationships, with God and with one another. Each sees something true, and the study holds all three together, but in an order, with what God gives and does coming before what we possess and perform, because that order is what keeps the image from being graded by our capacities and denied to the weak. The shortest answer is that to bear the image is to be God's representative in the world, made to show what he is like, a status he confers rather than a capacity we achieve.

faq.q: Does the image of God survive after the fall, or did sin destroy it?
faq.a: Both truths have to be held, and the study refuses to drop either. Sin defaced the image grievously, touching the reason, the will, and the relationships it was made to hold, and session three takes that ruin with full seriousness against a culture that will not name sin. But the image was not destroyed, and Scripture is plain about it, because after the fall and after the flood God still grounds the protection of human life in the image that fallen people bear, and James says we sin by cursing people presently made in God's likeness. The Reformed tradition captured this by speaking of the image in a broad sense, which survives, and a narrow sense, the original righteousness lost in the fall and restored in Christ. The pastoral payoff is enormous. A defaced image is not a destroyed one, which means no human being, however far gone, is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

faq.q: How is being conformed to Christ different from just self-improvement or becoming your best self?
faq.a: They look identical from the outside and are opposites at the root. Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same broken thing straining to fix itself by effort, which ends either in the exhaustion of failure or the pride of apparent success. Being conformed to the image of Christ, which session four unfolds, runs the other direction entirely, because the true image restores the defaced one from the outside, by grace, and the means is not striving but beholding. Paul says we are changed into his likeness from one degree of glory to another by beholding the glory of the Lord, because we become like what we look at. One is standing at a mirror watching yourself and trying harder. The other is standing at a window beholding Christ and being quietly remade by what you see. The difference is not the amount of effort but the direction the power comes from.

faq.q: Why does the study say the image is a gift and not something we earn? Do not humans do things that show they bear it?
faq.a: We do, but the order matters, and getting the order wrong is where the doctrine turns dangerous. If the image is first a capacity we possess or a performance we produce, then it comes in degrees, and whoever has less of the capacity has less of the image, and less, the logic whispers, of the worth. That is the machinery behind every dehumanization, the disabled, the demented, the unborn, the enemy all declared less than human. Genesis cuts against it by tying the image to what is simply passed from parent to child, given and inherited rather than achieved. So the study insists the image is first a status God confers, a call he issues, and a relationship he establishes, and only after that the capacities by which we live it out. A gift cannot be graded, a call does not depend on the strength to answer it, and a relationship holds the one who cannot respond, which is why the weakest person in any room bears the image whole.

faq.q: Is it not dangerous to tell people to see the image of God in their enemy or their abuser?
faq.a: It would be dangerous to teach it carelessly, and the study takes real pains not to. Seeing the image in someone does not mean trusting them, staying in reach of them, or declining to protect yourself and others from them, and where there is abuse the faithful and loving thing is safety, distance, and help, never a sentimental blindness dressed up as love. The study says this plainly and points toward real help. What seeing the image does mean is refusing to let even a genuine enemy become, in your eyes, less than human, a thing rather than a person, because the moment they do, your hatred has begun to deface the image in you. You can name someone's evil clearly, protect fully against it, work for justice, and still refuse to forget they are a defaced image-bearer and not a mere monster. That refusal is partly for your own sake, because it is what keeps the fight against evil from turning you into it.

faq.q: What does the study say about the worth of people with severe disabilities or dementia?
faq.a: It says their worth is exactly as full as anyone's, and it treats this as one of the places the doctrine matters most. The danger of grounding the image in a capacity like reason is that it leaves out the very people whose capacities are diminished, the profoundly disabled, the person lost to dementia, the infant. The study names that danger directly and refuses it, because the functional and relational views guard against it. A vocation can be given to a person who cannot presently exercise it, and a relationship can hold a person who cannot respond, the way a parent loves a newborn or a spouse keeps covenant with someone who no longer knows them. The image was conferred by God, held in a relationship he established, and it does not shrink because a person can do less. They bear it whole. For families who have felt written out of a doctrine preached as human rationality, this is not abstract, it is the defense they were owed.

faq.q: How does the image of God relate to Jesus? Why bring Christ into a doctrine from Genesis?
faq.a: Because the doctrine was never finished in Genesis and was always pointing to him. Genesis says Adam was made in the image. The New Testament says Christ is the image, and that one-word difference is the gospel. Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the true original of which Adam and all of us are copies, so that the most human face that ever existed is his. And this reaches into your life in two directions. Backward, it means the human race was patterned after the Son before he ever took our flesh. Forward, it means salvation is the defaced image being remade into his likeness, since Paul says believers are being conformed to the image of the Son. Session four unfolds all of it and lands on a reframe of the whole Christian life, that to be saved is not to become something other than human but to become human at last, the ruined likeness restored in the Person who wore our flesh without ruin.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not the image of God just a comforting story we tell to feel special?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study earns the right to answer it by taking the objection seriously rather than dodging it. It grants freely that humans are creatures formed from dust, kin to the animals, and it never pretends otherwise, because Genesis says so first. What it presses is not the biology but the gap the biology cannot fill, that the person who says a human is only a clever animal does not live as though that were true for a single waking hour. He is outraged by cruelty, grieved at a graveside, certain a child is worth more than a stone, and none of that follows from his own premise, because you cannot get infinite human worth out of atoms and instinct. The image is offered not as a flattering story but as the missing explanation, the only account that makes sense of the dignity everyone already assumes and no one can build from below. You do not have to believe it to notice that your own moral life is written in its language.

faq.q: Why does the writer keep implicating himself instead of just teaching the doctrine?
faq.a: Because the doctrine of the image is the one teaching in Scripture you cannot hold at arm's length, and pretending to would falsify it. The writer came to faith from atheism, so he held the other answer for years and knows it from the inside, and he confesses that he still assigns human worth on a sliding scale, generous toward the useful and impressive and stingy toward the inconvenient and ordinary. He writes from inside the indictment, not above it, because a study on human dignity that pointed only at other people's contempt would let everyone in the room off the hook and change no encounter. You cannot repent of a contempt you are still calling discernment, and you cannot call others to see the image in the faces they discount from a height that pretends you see every face rightly yourself. By keeping the writer inside the failure, the study makes it possible for the people actually in the room to have their eyes opened, which is the only place the doctrine ever does its work.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I know I struggle to see the image in certain people?
faq.a: That struggle is not a disqualification, it is the exact honesty the study runs on. This is not a study to be led by someone who has arrived at perfect sight, because no one has, and if you present yourself that way the room will perform agreement back at you and no one's eyes will open. Every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every objection is anticipated, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument, so the study was built to be led by ordinary people willing to go first. The real qualification is your willingness to name your own hardest face, the category of person your own instincts and your own tribe have trained you to look past, and to let the doctrine drag your eyes back to them alongside everyone else. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart about the tribal trap especially, and lead from inside the struggle to see, not from above it. Your honesty about the faces you find hard is the very thing that makes the room safe to be honest too.

faq.q: Does taking the image this seriously mean I have to agree with everyone or approve of everything people do?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful to keep those apart. Seeing the image in a person is not the same as trusting them, approving of them, or agreeing with them, and the image actually makes evil more serious rather than less, because to sin as an image-bearer is a betrayal of what you were made to be, and the study insists on full accountability rather than a cheap dignity that excuses everything. What the image refuses is not judgment of what people do but the despair and contempt that write a person off as less than human, beyond worth, fit to be discarded. You can name a wrong clearly, oppose it firmly, protect people from it fully, and still refuse to forget that the wrongdoer is a defaced image-bearer and not a monster. Holding both is not a contradiction, it is the whole art the doctrine teaches, taking evil seriously enough to name it and taking the image seriously enough never to erase the person underneath it.

timeline.event: Genesis 1 declares that God made humanity, male and female, in his own image and likeness, taking a title the surrounding empires reserved for the king alone and handing it to every human being, the most radical claim about human worth in the ancient world.

Genesis 3 narrates the defacing of the image, the creature made to represent God grasping instead to be God, fracturing the reason, the will, and the relationships the image was made to hold, so that the likeness is marred but, as later chapters show, never erased.

Genesis 9 grounds the sanctity of human life in the image, spoken over sinful survivors, proving that the fall did not destroy the likeness, since the protection of every remaining human life rests on an image that fallen people still bear.

Psalm 8 sings the paradox of the image, a dust creature made a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned with glory and honor, given dominion over the works of God's hands, the conferred royalty of humanity set to music.

Jesus of Nazareth lives as the true and perfect image of God in human flesh, the invisible God made visible, so that whoever has seen him has seen the Father, revealing the original of which Adam and all humanity were only ever the copy.

Paul names Christ the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, and describes salvation as believers being conformed to the image of the Son and changed into his likeness from one degree of glory to another.

Augustine locates the image in the rational structure of the soul, memory, understanding, and will, shaping the substantive reading that would dominate Christian thought for more than a thousand years, honoring human reason as the seat of the likeness.

Thomas Aquinas grounds the image in the intellect, the rational nature that distinguishes the human from the beasts, refining the substantive tradition into its classic scholastic form and tying human dignity closely to the capacity to reason.

John Calvin teaches that the fall did not annihilate the image but so corrupted it that what remains is a frightful deformity, and distinguishes the broad image that survives from the narrow image of righteousness lost in Adam and restored in Christ.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer lectures on Genesis in Berlin, published as Creation and Fall, recovering the image as relation and freedom-for the other, even as the regime that would murder him builds its own doctrine of lives unworthy of life.

Karl Barth develops in Church Dogmatics the relational reading of the image, locating it in the I and Thou of human relationship as a correspondence to the relationship God himself is, a theology forged against a century organized around racial hierarchy.

J. Richard Middleton publishes The Liberating Image, arguing in detail that Genesis 1 universalizes the royal-functional image against ancient Near Eastern ideology, recovering the doctrine's original force as a liberation and a charter of universal human dignity.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here, because it takes a certain courage to look honestly at what a human being is worth and why. Before we start, three things. First, this is not a study about human dignity in the abstract, which is easy to affirm and costs nothing. It is about whether we can see the image of God in the specific people we would rather not, so the only person whose sight any of us is responsible for in this room is our own. Second, this doctrine belongs to no political side, and we are going to let it cut against every tribe, including our own, so come ready to have your team's blind spot named as honestly as your opponents', and hold your grip loosely. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of it. He came to faith from atheism, so he held the other answer, and he admits he still grades human worth on a sliding scale, generous to the useful and stingy toward the inconvenient, and so will we. We are not seeing perfectly and teaching the rest of you to catch up. We are all still learning to see. One thing that matters, and I mean it. If anything we touch tonight comes near a real wound you carry, a loss, a crisis, an abuser, you do not have to perform anything, and I am available to talk privately and to help. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this session says. Now let us bring it down off the page and into the actual week each of us walked in from and will walk back into, into real faces and real encounters, because a doctrine of the image that changes no encounter on Monday was never believed on Sunday.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it does not resolve, because this doctrine convicts and then sends you out still carrying it rather than tying a bow on it. Take the weight home instead of setting it down at the door. Try the practice this week, with a real person, even badly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And come back ready to be honest, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go, and remember, there are no ordinary people, none of us has ever locked eyes with a mere mortal, and my door is open if any of you needs it. Thank you for the courage it took to be in this conversation.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about seeing your own blind spot and refusing the tribal capture of the doctrine, and walk session one's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, The Image the Kings Kept for Themselves, with extra time on the ancient background and the democratization of the image.
Week 3: Session 2, What the Image Is, part one, the three views laid out and the danger of grounding worth in a capacity.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, the order that holds the three views together and the pastoral payoff for the disabled and the weak, with care for anyone it touches closely.
Week 5: Session 3, Defaced but Not Destroyed, holding the seriousness of sin and the surviving dignity together.
Week 6: Session 4, The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming, formation as restoration by beholding rather than self-improvement by striving.
Week 7: Session 5, The Image in the Street, walking the list of the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, and the person who annoys you, with the tribal trap named in both directions.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and whose face each person is going home to finally see, closing in the God who assigns a worth we cannot revoke.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the image taken out of the palace and the argument over what it is and why it decides who counts as fully human.
Week 2: Session 3, Defaced but Not Destroyed, the image marred by the fall and never erased.
Week 3: Session 4, The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming, Christ the image and the restoration of the ruined likeness.
Week 4: Session 5, The Image in the Street, plus a short integration close in the dignity that stands over every tribe and belongs to none.

plan: Week 1: Session 1, The Image the Kings Kept for Themselves.
Week 2: Session 2, What the Image Is, and Why the Argument Matters.
Week 3: Session 3, Defaced but Not Destroyed.
Week 4: Session 4, The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming.

bibliography.title: The Liberating Image: The Imago Dei in Genesis 1
bibliography.author: J. Richard Middleton
bibliography.note: The scholarly spine of the study's reading of Genesis, arguing that the creation account universalizes the royal-functional image against ancient Near Eastern ideology, taking the divine image out of the palace and giving it to everyone. Anchors sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Creation and Fall: A Theological Exposition of Genesis 1-3
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's 1932 to 1933 Berlin lectures on Genesis, recovering the image as relation and freedom-for the other, delivered as the Nazi regime built its doctrine of lives unworthy of life. Background for sessions 2, 3, and 5. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them.

bibliography.title: Church Dogmatics, III/1 and III/2
bibliography.author: Karl Barth
bibliography.note: Barth's development of the relational reading of the image, located in the I and Thou of human relationship as a correspondence to the being of God. Dense but foundational for the relational view in session 2. Leader to weigh carefully and confirm before pressing any specific argument.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: General background on the moral argument and human dignity, useful for the skeptic's objection in session 1 that worth cannot be built from below. The line about there being no ordinary people comes from Lewis's sermon The Weight of Glory, not this book, and should be cited to that source.

bibliography.title: The Weight of Glory
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The sermon containing the claim that you have never talked to a mere mortal and that your neighbor is the holiest object presented to your senses, quoted at the end of session 5. The primary source for that line, to be cited accurately.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Calvin's teaching that the fall did not annihilate the image but corrupted it into a frightful deformity, and his distinction between the broad and narrow senses of the image. The historical anchor for session 3. Leader to handle the precise wording with care.

bibliography.title: Dignity and Destiny: Humanity in the Image of God
bibliography.author: John F. Kilner
bibliography.note: A thorough evangelical study of the image that stresses grounding human dignity in God's conferring rather than in human capacities, closely aligned with the study's insistence on the order. Supports sessions 2 and 3. Leader to confirm specific claims.

bibliography.title: In the Beginning... Creation and the Priestly History
bibliography.author: Claus Westermann
bibliography.note: Representative of major critical Genesis scholarship on the image and its ancient context, offered as a category for leaders who want the exegetical background. Leader to select and confirm specific claims rather than treating any single reading as settled.

bibliography.title: Bonhoeffer: Pastor, Martyr, Prophet, Spy
bibliography.author: Eric Metaxas
bibliography.note: A widely read biography giving the historical setting of Bonhoeffer's resistance to a regime built on denying the image, useful background for session 5's account of the doctrine as resistance. A popular account, leader to weigh against primary sources and confirm details.

bibliography.title: The Book of Genesis, Chapters 1-17 (New International Commentary)
bibliography.author: Victor P. Hamilton
bibliography.note: A standard evangelical commentary on the creation and fall texts, useful for leaders wanting careful verse-level grounding for sessions 1 and 3. A reference to consult rather than read straight through. Leader to confirm before pressing any specific argument as the study's own.

bibliography.title: Genesis
bibliography.author: the book of Genesis
bibliography.note: The primary biblical text underlying the whole study, chapters 1, 3, 5, and 9, where the image is made, defaced, inherited, and protected. The foundation to be read and not only cited, especially the first nine chapters.

The Weight of Glory, C. S. Lewis, especially the closing pages on there being no ordinary people, for anyone who wants the heart of session 5 in a single unforgettable sermon.

glossary.definition: The Latin phrase for the image of God, the biblical teaching that human beings are made in God's image and likeness, given a dignity and a vocation no other creature has. The subject of the whole study, drawn from Genesis 1:26-27.

The Hebrew word translated image in Genesis 1, ordinarily used for a statue set up to represent a god in a temple. It casts the human being as God's statue placed in the temple of his creation, made to represent him and show what he is like.

The Hebrew word translated likeness in Genesis 1, paired with tselem. Most interpreters read the two as a poetic parallelism naming a single reality rather than two separate things, guarding against building large doctrines on a small grammatical difference.

The recognition that Genesis takes the divine image, reserved in the surrounding empires for the king alone, and extends it to every human being, male and female, slave and free, the liberation J. Richard Middleton names in The Liberating Image.

The classic reading, running from Augustine and Aquinas through most of the tradition, that the image is a quality inside us, most often reason or the rational soul. It honors what is distinctive in humans but risks grounding worth in a capacity some possess less of.

The reading, closest to Genesis in its ancient context, that the image is a vocation, the calling to represent God and steward his creation as his royal representatives. It protects the worth of those who cannot exercise the role, since a vocation can be conferred and held in trust.

The reading, developed by Barth and Bonhoeffer, that the image is found in the relationships we stand in, with God and with one another. It protects the worth of those who cannot respond, since a relationship God establishes holds a person even when every capacity fails.

The two-sided truth about the fall's effect on the image, that sin marred it grievously in every part yet never erased it, so that fallen human beings still bear the image, which is why no person is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

Calvin's distinction between the broad image, the human constitution that survives the fall, and the narrow image, the original righteousness lost in Adam and restored in Christ, which lets Scripture say both that the image remains and that it must be renewed.

Jesus Christ, whom Paul calls the image of the invisible God, not a bearer of the image but the image itself, the true original of which Adam and all humanity are copies, and the pattern into which the defaced image is being remade.

The New Testament description of salvation as the defaced image being restored into the likeness of Christ, changed from one degree of glory to another by beholding him, so that Christian formation is the ruined humanity being made truly human at last.

The biblical principle that we are formed into the image of whatever holds our gaze and worship, so that the Christian is changed by beholding Christ, and, on the sobering flip side, deformed into the image of any idol we fix our eyes on instead.

The failure of turning the image of God into a weapon for one political side, wielded to defend the people a tribe already favors and to indict only its opponents, which empties the doctrine, since a true doctrine of the image cuts against every tribe with the same blade.

The conviction, put memorably by C. S. Lewis, that because every human bears the image, there are no ordinary or disposable people and no face safe to despise, so that how we treat any person is how we treat their Maker.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The Bible's oldest and most radical claim about people is that they are made in the image of God, and almost nobody stops to ask what that means or why it should change how we treat a single human being. quoteCards: Every empire around Israel kept the divine image in the palace. Genesis took it out and handed it to everyone.
The argument about what the image is turns out to be the argument about who gets counted as fully human.
A defaced image is still an image. The signature is still under the ruin.
To be saved is not to become something other than human. It is to become human at last.
We are changed into his likeness not by striving at the mirror but by beholding him at the window.
The image cuts against every tribe with the same blade, or it has become a tribe in robes.
You have never locked eyes with a mere mortal.
How you treat the image is how you treat the One imaged. There are no ordinary people.
